name: IoT / device telemetry rollups + anomaly windows
parent_research_topic: Beava use cases — current and potential applications of beava as a real-time feature server

domain_fit.domain_name: IoT / device telemetry rollups and per-device anomaly windows (industrial IoT, connected vehicles, smart energy/metering, building automation)
domain_fit.one_line_definition: A reliability / fleet-ops / IIoT engineer or a predictive-maintenance ML platform team computes per-device rolling counters (errors, sensor extremes, connectivity drops) and per-fleet distribution / z-score features over second-to-minute windows, and serves them to maintenance dashboards, alerting rules, and ML scorers with sub-second freshness.
domain_fit.representative_jobs_to_be_done: 1) Power per-device anomaly windows: 'this pump's vibration_RMS over the last 60 s is >3 sigma above its 7-day baseline AND error_count_5m > 5 — open a maintenance ticket and bias the inference scorer.' 2) Maintain predictive-maintenance feature precursors that ML models read at inference time — rolling mean / std / min / max of sensor channels, time-since-last-anomaly, delta-since-last-cleaning, error-rate velocity — at second-grain freshness rather than the 5–15 min lag of warehouse-resident features. 3) Feed fleet-wide live dashboards (connected-vehicle ops, smart-meter outage maps, building energy heatmaps) with rolling counters of error events, connectivity drops, and out-of-band sensor readings, refreshed every few seconds. 4) Provide a 'hot tier' of per-device features that sits between an MQTT/Kafka broker and the time-series database (Influx / Timescale / ClickHouse / ADX), giving online scorers and rules engines microsecond access without round-tripping to the TSDB. 5) Compute per-fleet z-score / percentile features (current-device-value vs. fleet distribution) so that 'this meter is reading 4 sigma above its neighborhood right now' is a single feature read instead of an ad-hoc OLAP query.
domain_fit.event_shapes: MQTT / Sparkplug / OPC-UA bridged messages, AWS IoT / Azure IoT Hub built-in routes, Tesla-style fleet-telemetry frames, smart-meter AMI uploads. Typical shapes: sensor_reading {ts, device_id, channel ('vibration_rms' | 'temp_c' | 'pressure_kpa' | 'rpm'), value, quality_code}, device_status {ts, device_id, fw_version, uptime_s, rssi}, connectivity_event {ts, device_id, event_type ('connect' | 'disconnect' | 'reconnect' | 'last_will'), reason}, error_event {ts, device_id, error_code, severity}, command_ack {ts, device_id, cmd_id, latency_ms, result}, position_frame {ts, vehicle_id, lat, lon, speed, accel, brake_pressure, motor_temp, cell_v}, meter_reading {ts, meter_id, kwh, vrms, irms, freq_hz, power_factor, tamper_flag}. Tesla Fleet Telemetry pushes at 500 ms cadence; Rivian streams over 5,500 telemetry signals every 5 seconds per vehicle. Smart-meter AMI is far slower (15-min interval reads), with bursts on outage / tamper events.
domain_fit.feature_shapes: Heavy use of count, rate / velocity, recency, distribution, and distance / delta primitives in tumbling and sliding windows, plus per-fleet population statistics. Per-device: count(error_event, 1m/5m/1h/24h), velocity(error_event / minute), rate(connectivity_drop / hour), recency(last_error_ts), delta_since_last_anomaly, distribution(sensor_value over 60s / 5m / 1h — mean, std, min, max, p50/p95/p99 via t-digest), time_in_state (cumulative seconds the device has been in 'degraded' or 'offline'), max-seen and min-seen sensor over the trailing window. Per-fleet / per-cohort (geohash, line, model, fw_version, substation): n_unique(active_device_id, 5m), distribution(sensor_value across the fleet right now → z-score lookup), count(devices_in_alert), distribution(uptime_s). The two flagship features for predictive maintenance are 'this device vs its own past' (rolling z-score per device) and 'this device vs its peers right now' (fleet z-score) — both expressible as count + distribution primitives.
domain_fit.entity_grain: Composite and high-cardinality. Primary: device_id / IMEI / MAC / serial / VIN / meter_id. Secondary: (device_id, channel) for per-channel rolling stats, (device_id, error_code) for per-error counters. Cohort keys: model, fw_version, site_id / facility_id / substation_id, geohash / H3 cell, customer_id (for multi-tenant device fleets), production line. Connected-vehicle fleet ops typically pivots on vehicle_id and (vehicle_id, subsystem); smart energy pivots on meter_id and (meter_id, channel); industrial IoT pivots on (asset_id, sensor_id).
domain_fit.window_semantics_required: All three. Sliding 60 s / 5 m / 1 h windows for 'rolling mean / std / min / max' anomaly-window features (the canonical predictive-maintenance feature shape — sensor_mean, sensor_std over the trailing window). Tumbling 1 m / 5 m / 1 h / 24 h windows for dashboards, SLA counters, and warehouse hand-off. Session windows for connectivity (a 'connected session' starts at MQTT CONNECT and ends at the configurable inactivity / last-will timeout — natural session window). Approximate aggregates are acceptable and often preferred: HLL for 'distinct devices reporting in last 5 m' at fleet scale, CMS / Top-K for 'top-N noisiest devices right now', t-digest for sensor-value percentiles, EWMA for smoothed rolling means. Exact counts are required only where the feature is consumed by a billing or regulatory counter (kWh totalizer, tamper-flag count for revenue protection).
domain_fit.exactly_once_or_idempotency_needs: At-least-once is the operational default and is acceptable for the vast majority of anomaly / predictive-maintenance features — a slightly over-counted error_event does not derail an ML scorer. MQTT QoS 1 is the de-facto standard at the broker layer and already produces at-least-once delivery; SDK-level dedup on (device_id, message_id) is common. Strict exactly-once is required only where the counter is the source-of-truth for billing (kWh, energy export) or revenue-protection (tamper detection), which most deployments push to a downstream regulated meter-data-management system rather than the hot feature tier.

technical_fit.latency_budget: Read p99 <10 ms is comfortable for online inference scorers (predictive-maintenance models reading 20–80 features per device per scoring decision); <100 ms is the operational target for control-room dashboards and rules-engine evaluation; <1 s is the published target for 'early-warning maintenance dashboards' (academic work cites 1 s as the canonical real-time anomaly-window budget). beava's sub-ms TCP+msgpack get / batch_get sits well inside all three, and is comparable to Aerospike's published p95 ~2 ms feature-lookup latency.
technical_fit.feature_freshness_sla: Sub-second to a few seconds end-to-end is the differentiating goal. Tesla Fleet Telemetry streams at 500 ms cadence; Rivian streams 5,500 signals every 5 s per vehicle; OPC-UA / Sparkplug 'report by exception' is sub-second. The competitive gap to close is the warehouse / TSDB hop: continuous aggregates in TimescaleDB and ClickHouse materialized views are pre-computed on a refresh schedule (typically seconds-to-minutes), and most predictive-maintenance ML pipelines today read features that are minutes-stale because the rolling window lives in the warehouse rather than in-memory. beava's push-on-event model targets the same second-grain SLA that the broker-and-Flink stack provides today, without requiring Flink.
technical_fit.throughput_profile: Heavily site-dependent. A single industrial facility runs hundreds-to-thousands of OPC-UA tags at 100 ms–1 s cadence, often 1k–50k EPS aggregate. A connected-vehicle fleet at Tesla / Rivian scale is much higher: a 500 ms cadence per car times millions of cars implies aggregate volumes in the millions of EPS at the platform layer (Rivian publicly reports 88% volume reduction via Flink-based filtering before downstream). A national smart-meter AMI fleet of 10M meters at 15-min interval reads is only ~11k EPS aggregate but bursts under outages; Southern Company manages 4.6M smart meters. Cloud platform anchors: AWS IoT Core meters per-message in 5 KB increments; Azure IoT Hub S2 caps at 6M messages/day/unit (~70 EPS) and S3 at 300M messages/day/unit (~3.5k EPS) — these are tenant-level caps, not platform caps. A single beava node at ~684k EPS (M4, TCP+msgpack, parallel=16) sits between a single industrial site (overkill) and a national connected-vehicle platform (still requires sharding). [uncertain]
technical_fit.read_to_write_ratio: Write-heavy at the ingestion tier (every telemetry frame is a write, every 500 ms–15 min depending on domain) — the README's framing of telemetry as 'write-heavy' is accurate. Reads are mostly batched (the inference scorer pulls 20–80 features per device per scoring tick, the dashboard pulls 50–500 features per refresh) so a get_many / batch_get surface matters more than raw single-key read throughput. Net: 5–50x more writes than reads in most fleet deployments, inverted only when an online scorer is running per-device every second.
technical_fit.state_size_estimate: Dominated by device_id × (channel, error_code) cardinality, which is the operationally explosive axis. A 100k-device fleet with 20 channels and a handful of rolling-window features per channel lands at ~10–50 GB hot state (assuming ~500 B per per-entity feature row including t-digest sketches). A 1M-device fleet (large utility / Tier-1 OEM) is ~100–500 GB and starts to exceed a single-box RAM budget. A 10M+ fleet (national smart-meter rollout, hyperscaler IoT tenant) requires sharding regardless of engine. beava's in-memory-only model fits a single-site or single-region deployment well, but a national / hyperscaler-scale deployment exceeds what beava v0 can hold in-process without external sharding. [uncertain]
technical_fit.cardinality_pattern: Slowly-growing on device_id (bounded by fleet size and replacement rate). Bounded on channel, error_code, fw_version, site_id, model. Slowly-growing on (device_id, channel) and (device_id, error_code) — these are the dominant memory consumers. Explosive only on the message-id / event-id axis (which beava does not retain individually) and on geohash if the resolution is high. The classic 'high-cardinality observability' problem (Honeycomb, Chronosphere) maps directly onto this domain: per-device features are exactly the high-cardinality dimension that aggregated TSDB metrics throw away.
technical_fit.typical_state_lifecycle_and_ttl: Seconds-to-minutes for the rolling-window features that drive online inference. 1–24 hours for fleet-ops dashboards and incident triage. 7–30 days for predictive-maintenance feature history at the hot tier — beyond that, the warehouse / lakehouse owns the archive. Connectivity-session state lives only for the duration of the session (MQTT keepalive timeout, typically 60–300 s). Smart-meter use cases retain rolling features longer (30–90 days for billing-related anomaly history). Connected-vehicle telemetry is GDPR-constrained — driver-identifiable rolling features must obey configured retention.
technical_fit.typical_feature_count_per_decision: 20–80 features per online predictive-maintenance inference decision (rolling mean / std / min / max across ~5–15 sensor channels = 20–60 features, plus error / connectivity counters and fleet-z-score lookups = another 10–20). Fleet-ops dashboard refresh batches 100–1000 features at once. Connected-vehicle anomaly detectors typically read fewer but stricter latency features (5–20 per vehicle, scored every 1–5 s).
technical_fit.durability_requirements: Best-effort to crash-safe. The anomaly-window feature tier is derived state — the source of truth is the broker (MQTT/Kafka) and the TSDB. Losing 5 minutes of rolling-window state on restart degrades the next few anomaly decisions but is recoverable by replay from the broker or by re-warming from the TSDB. beava's WAL + snapshot model is adequate. Regulator-grade durability is required only where the same counter feeds billing (smart-meter kWh, energy-export totalizer) or safety-critical decisions (connected-vehicle brake/battery anomaly flagged for recall) — those should stay in the regulated meter-data-management or safety-of-the-intended-functionality (SOTIF) pipeline, not in beava.
technical_fit.deployment_topology_fit: Strong fit for single-binary edge / on-prem industrial gateway (alongside the MQTT broker or OPC-UA bridge on a factory-floor box), and for regional sidecar-next-to-broker topologies (one beava per region, behind a Kafka-MQTT bridge). Strong fit for the 'feature aggregator above the TSDB, not replacement' positioning in the description — beava sits between MQTT/Kafka and Influx/Timescale/ClickHouse. Weaker fit for multi-region active-active (a connected-vehicle global fleet, a hyperscaler IoT tenant) because beava v0 has no in-process sharding and no replication. The single-binary, no-broker-required nature is the natural advantage for an industrial-edge gateway where Flink / Spark / Kafka are operationally too heavy.

commercial_fit.who_buys: (a) Industrial reliability / predictive-maintenance engineering teams at PTC ThingWorx, Siemens Insights Hub (ex-MindSphere), AVEVA, Aspen Tech, GE Digital, Rockwell FactoryTalk customers — buying or replacing the per-asset anomaly layer of an IIoT platform. (b) Fleet-ops and vehicle-anomaly platform teams at OEMs (Tesla, Rivian, Volkswagen, Ford Pro) building per-vehicle live feature serving for cybersecurity, battery, and powertrain anomalies. (c) Smart-metering / AMI engineering teams at utilities (Southern Company-class, Enel, EDF, Octopus, Itron, Landis+Gyr) building tamper-detection and outage-anomaly features. (d) Smart-building / facilities engineering teams (Johnson Controls, Siemens BT, Honeywell, Carrier, Schneider EcoStruxure) computing per-zone HVAC / lighting anomaly features. (e) IoT platform vendors themselves (Particle, Balena, ThingsBoard, Akenza) considering an embedded 'hot feature tier' inside their fleet management product. The buyer in this domain is reliability / fleet-ops / IoT platform engineering — not the data team and not the risk team.
commercial_fit.market_size_signal: Predictive maintenance market sized at $9.2–14.3 B in 2025 by various analysts, projected to $40–98 B by 2030–2034 (Fortune Business Insights $13.65B → $97.37B at 24.3% CAGR; Grand View Research $14.29B → $98.16B at 27.9% CAGR; MarkNtel $10.93B (2024) → $41.90B at 25.1% CAGR; Precedence $9.21B → $94.27B at 26.2%). Industrial IoT platform market sized at $11.1 B in 2025, projected to $30.3 B by 2033 at 13.4% CAGR (SNS Insider). Connected-vehicle technology / connected-car market sized at $45–87 B in 2025, projected to $364 B by 2035 at ~15% CAGR. Specific vendor revenue context: PTC ThingWorx hit $29M Q2 with 33% YoY growth at one point; Siemens MindSphere rebranded to Insights Hub in 2023 after failing to become 'the OS of IoT'; GE Predix never reached its claimed $5B external revenue. The largest-spending sub-segment is connected vehicles (multi-billion-dollar OEM telemetry programs), followed by industrial predictive maintenance, then smart energy. [uncertain]
commercial_fit.urgency_drivers: 1) AI-driven predictive maintenance and SOTIF (safety of the intended functionality) for connected vehicles need rolling sensor features at sub-second freshness — the buyer can no longer accept the 5–15 min warehouse lag for safety-adjacent decisions. 2) Energy-grid stability and outage response under renewables penetration require sub-second per-meter / per-substation anomaly windows. 3) Industrial IoT platforms have consolidated (620+ platforms → cloud hyperscalers + a few specialists, per IoT Analytics) and the remaining buyers want OSS, in-VPC, single-binary alternatives to Flink-on-Kafka. 4) Apache Iceberg / lakehouse adoption means buyers want to keep the warehouse / TSDB layer cold and offload rolling-window compute to a hot tier they can self-host. 5) Connected-vehicle cyber-anomaly detection (UN R155 / R156, ISO/SAE 21434) is an active regulatory driver pushing OEMs toward per-vehicle live feature serving. 6) Edge / on-prem hosting is increasingly required because telemetry data is industrially sensitive (manufacturing process IP, vehicle telemetry, building-occupancy data).
commercial_fit.regulatory_or_audit_constraints: Connected vehicles: GDPR + EDPB Guidelines 01/2020 on connected vehicles (driver-PII retention limits, in-region processing, right-to-erasure), UN R155/R156 cyber-management for type approval, ISO/SAE 21434 cybersecurity engineering. Smart energy / AMI: NERC CIP for North-American grid, EU Network Code on Cybersecurity, country-specific revenue-meter standards (UK SMETS2, US ANSI C12), GDPR for residential meter data. Industrial: IEC 62443 for OT cybersecurity, sector-specific (FDA 21 CFR Part 11 in pharma, HACCP in food). SOC 2 is table-stakes for any SaaS slice. The biggest beava-specific gap is the lack of TLS / auth in v0 — disqualifying for any deployment that crosses an OT/IT boundary, which is the entire IIoT and AMI install base outside of a strictly trusted gateway VLAN.
commercial_fit.time_to_value_signal: Fast — 2–5 days to a working 'per-device rolling mean / std + error_velocity + fleet-z-score' demo on a laptop using beava's @bv.event + @bv.table primitives, with an MQTT-to-beava shim ingesting Sparkplug or AWS IoT-formatted JSON. 2–4 weeks to a production pilot on a single industrial gateway or per-region fleet-ops sidecar, gated mostly by adding TLS/auth (v0 gap), wiring up TTL/eviction policy for the device_id × channel cardinality, and bridging from MQTT or Sparkplug into beava's HTTP/TCP push surface. Connected-vehicle and smart-energy pilots are slower (4–12 weeks) because of regulatory review.

competition.incumbents: Generic streaming / feature stack the buyer would otherwise assemble: Apache Kafka + Apache Flink (the de-facto IIoT stream pipeline cited in Confluent, Kai Waehner, Rivian, and Volkswagen case studies); Spark Structured Streaming; Materialize, RisingWave for streaming SQL aggregates; Redis (counters, sorted-sets, RedisTimeSeries module) and Aerospike (Aerospike-as-feature-store for PlayStation-class personalization, sub-millisecond p95) at the hot feature tier; Tecton / Hopsworks / Chalk / Feast / Fennel as managed online feature stores (Hopsworks publicly used by Siemens / Safran for manufacturing AI governance; Chalk explicitly lists predictive maintenance as a target). At the TSDB tier: InfluxDB (purpose-built for IoT, Rust+Arrow rewrite in v3), TimescaleDB / Tiger Data (Postgres extension with continuous aggregates), ClickHouse (columnar OLAP with materialized views), QuestDB, Azure Data Explorer (ADX), Apache Pinot, Apache Druid.
competition.competitive_incumbent_per_domain: Industrial IoT platforms: PTC ThingWorx, Siemens Insights Hub (ex-MindSphere), GE Digital APM / Predix (largely deprecated externally), AVEVA, Rockwell FactoryTalk, Bosch IoT Suite, Hitachi Lumada, Cognite Data Fusion, Uptake, AspenTech (acquired by Emerson). Connected vehicles: vehicle OEM in-house stacks (Tesla Fleet Telemetry, Rivian + Volkswagen on Kafka+Flink via RV Tech joint venture, Ford Pro Intelligence, Mercedes Daimler), Wejo (defunct), Otonomo, High Mobility, Mobileye platform, Upstream (automotive cyber-anomaly), Teslemetry. Smart energy / AMI: Itron, Landis+Gyr, Honeywell Elster, Siemens Smart Infrastructure, Trilliant, Aclara, Sensus, Schneider Electric ADMS / EcoStruxure Grid, Oracle MDM. Building automation: Johnson Controls OpenBlue, Siemens Building Technologies, Honeywell Forge, Schneider EcoStruxure Building, Carrier Abound. Telemetry platforms (observability adjacent): Datadog (with Watchdog anomaly detection), Splunk Observability Cloud (formerly SignalFx, high-cardinality second-resolution datastore), Honeycomb, Chronosphere, Last9. None of these is a pure feature server — beava's natural position is the per-device 'hot feature tier' sitting underneath them, fed by their broker and read by their scorer / dashboard / rules engine.
competition.beava_differentiator: 1) Sub-second feature freshness vs. the incumbents' 5–60 min materialized-view / continuous-aggregate refresh — TimescaleDB continuous aggregates and ClickHouse materialized views are explicitly pre-computed on a refresh schedule, not push-on-event, which is the freshness gap beava closes. 2) 50+ aggregation primitives — count, velocity, recency, rolling mean/std/min/max, distance, distribution (t-digest), z-score-against-fleet — match the literal feature engineering shapes that academic predictive-maintenance papers use (rolling_mean, rolling_std, time-since-last-X), without writing Flink SQL or Lua-on-Redis. 3) Single binary, no broker / no ETL — fits an industrial-edge gateway or per-region sidecar where Kafka+Flink is operationally too heavy and OT teams refuse to operate. 4) Push-on-event over HTTP/JSON :8080 and framed TCP+msgpack :8081 maps directly to how MQTT-to-Kafka bridges, OPC-UA bridges, and AWS IoT / Azure IoT Hub egress routes already produce events. 5) Apache-2.0, no open-core — important for IoT platform vendors (Particle, Balena, ThingsBoard, Akenza) who might embed beava without dragging in a competitor's managed cloud. 6) Distance / delta / recency primitives are first-class — 'delta_since_last_anomaly' and 'time_since_last_error' are exactly the predictive-maintenance feature precursors the description calls out, and these are hand-rolled on Redis and slow in a TSDB.
competition.where_beava_loses_today: 1) No TLS, no auth in v0 — disqualifying for any deployment that crosses an OT/IT boundary or sits outside a strictly trusted VLAN; this rules out essentially all production IIoT, smart-meter, and connected-vehicle deployments outside of a gateway-internal use. 2) No in-process sharding and no replication — a national smart-meter fleet, a Tier-1 OEM connected-vehicle program, or a multi-region IoT platform tenant exceeds a single beava node and must hand-shard externally. 3) In-memory only with refuse-on-network-FS — adequate for a derived hot tier but rules out using beava as the authoritative meter-reading store (which must be regulator-grade durable anyway, so this is a positioning constraint more than a real loss). 4) No SQL / ad-hoc query — incumbents like ClickHouse, ADX, Druid let SREs cut new fleet queries on the fly; beava only serves features it has been told to compute, forcing the buyer to declare features in advance. 5) No native MQTT / OPC-UA / Sparkplug ingestion — buyers will need a small bridge (MQTT-to-HTTP, MQTT-to-TCP+msgpack) which is ~50 lines but is a friction. 6) No native triggers — alerting and ticket-cutting requires polling or an external rules engine; this is the same gap called out elsewhere and is acute here because anomaly windows literally exist to fire actions. 7) No multi-tenancy primitives (namespaces, per-tenant quotas) for IoT platform vendors embedding beava across many customer fleets. 8) No optional event-archive sink (S3 / Parquet / Iceberg) so the buyer must dual-write to a TSDB / lakehouse for cold tier.
competition.integration_surface: Producers: MQTT (HiveMQ, EMQX, Mosquitto, AWS IoT Core, Azure IoT Hub) via a small MQTT-to-beava bridge — payloads are typically JSON or Sparkplug-B protobuf and map cleanly to beava's HTTP/JSON :8080 or TCP+msgpack :8081 surface; OPC-UA bridges (HiveMQ Edge, Kepware, Unified Namespace gateways); Kafka / Kinesis for buyers already on a streaming bus (Rivian / VW pattern); direct push from edge gateways and PLCs via HTTP; AWS IoT Rules / Azure IoT Hub routes that forward to an HTTP endpoint. Consumers: predictive-maintenance ML scorers (XGBoost / LightGBM / LSTM / GRU per academic literature) reading via batch_get; fleet-ops dashboards (Grafana, custom React/SSE, ThingsBoard widgets); rules engines and alerting (Alertmanager, PagerDuty, ServiceNow); SCADA / DCS HMI overlays; CMMS / EAM ticket-cutters (IBM Maximo, SAP PM, Infor EAM). beava's HTTP/TCP-push model is closer to the AWS IoT Rules / Azure IoT Hub egress shape than to a Kafka-only feature store, which is an advantage when the buyer already uses a hyperscaler IoT broker.
competition.scoring_engine_coupling: Both. An ML scorer (XGBoost / LightGBM / LSTM / GRU / 1D-CNN for vibration / Isolation Forest for univariate anomaly) consumes per-device rolling features at inference time, and an external rules engine (Drools, FactoryTalk Live Data, vendor-specific PLC logic, SCADA alarms, AWS IoT Rules) consumes the same features for threshold-based alerting. beava remains the pure feature backend in both cases; the scoring and rule-evaluation live elsewhere.

adoption_signals.existing_public_users_or_case_studies: No public users of beava on this use case identified. [uncertain] Comparable production references at incumbents: Rivian + Volkswagen (RV Tech) publicly process >5,500 telemetry signals every 5 s per vehicle via Kafka + Flink and achieved 88% volume reduction via early-pipeline filtering / feature engineering (Kai Waehner blog, January 2026); Tesla Fleet Telemetry publishes a 500 ms streaming cadence; Southern Company manages 4.6M smart meters on a Databricks-based architecture; PlayStation runs its online personalization feature store on Aerospike with p95 2 ms feature-lookup latency (Aerospike case study); Siemens, Intel, and Safran use Hopsworks as a feature store for manufacturing / industrial ML; Chalk explicitly lists predictive maintenance as one of its primary verticals; ThingsBoard has named smart-metering / smart-energy use cases; InfluxData publishes IIoT and predictive maintenance as named solution slices. These are all 'comparable platform' references, not beava-specific.
adoption_signals.community_discussions: No beava-specific Discord / GitHub Discussion / RFC threads on IoT / device telemetry located. [uncertain] Broader community signal is strong: HiveMQ blog series on MQTT-vs-Kafka and MQTT-Sparkplug-vs-OPC-UA (active 2024–2026); Kai Waehner's IIoT data-streaming series (Confluent / independent, 2022–2026); ManufacturingTomorrow, IoT For All, IoT Analytics reports on platform consolidation; r/IOT and r/dataengineering threads on warehouse-vs-stream-vs-hot-tier hybrids for telemetry; academic literature on rolling-window predictive-maintenance features is dense (MDPI, ScienceDirect, Springer 2024–2025).
adoption_signals.examples_or_demos_in_repo: No dedicated IoT / device-telemetry / predictive-maintenance demo identified in the repository. /tmp/docker-desktop-root/run/desktop/mnt/host/d/Code/Beava/beava/python/beava/demos/ contains only adtech, ecommerce, and fraud demos as of the current snapshot. A purpose-built demo (per-device rolling vibration_rms mean/std, error_velocity, time_since_last_anomaly, fleet-z-score) would be a natural addition and is achievable on top of the existing @bv.event + @bv.table primitives without server-side changes. [uncertain]
adoption_signals.adversarial_pressure_level: Mostly passive with localized adversarial pockets. The core predictive-maintenance / fleet-ops slice is passive load — drift comes from equipment wear, fw upgrades, sensor recalibration, and seasonal patterns, not from an attacker. Two slices are adversarial: connected-vehicle cybersecurity (CAN-bus injection, OTA tampering, UN R155 scope) and smart-meter tamper / revenue protection (energy theft, magnetic interference, terminal compromise) — both require feature drift expectations comparable to fraud (use cases 1a–4). The bulk of the deployment is the passive-load case.

risk_and_non_goals.non_goals: 1) Replacing the time-series database — beava is the hot, declared-feature tier above the TSDB, not a substitute for InfluxDB / TimescaleDB / ClickHouse / ADX / Pinot / Druid; the description explicitly calls this out. 2) Replacing the broker — beava does not replace MQTT, Kafka, AWS IoT Core, or Azure IoT Hub at the message-bus layer; it sits behind one of them. 3) Long historical lookback (>30–90 days) — beava is in-memory only; the lakehouse / TSDB owns the cold archive and the model-training feature backfill. 4) Ad-hoc analyst SQL across the fleet (e.g., 'show me all pumps whose vibration > 5σ over the last quarter') — that is OLAP / TSDB territory. 5) Source-of-truth for revenue meters or safety-critical decisions — kWh totals and safety-flagged anomalies belong in regulated MDM / SOTIF pipelines with stricter durability and audit. 6) Edge inference / on-device model serving — beava is a feature server, not a model runtime; the inference engine (ONNX Runtime, NVIDIA Triton, custom MCU code) lives separately. 7) Cross-entity join queries across devices × sites × customers — feature-server scope is per-entity, not cross-entity.
risk_and_non_goals.open_engineering_gaps: Concrete features beava would need to ship to be production-grade for this domain, roughly in priority order: 1) TLS termination and an auth model (token / mTLS) on :8081 and :8090 — without these, beava cannot cross any OT/IT boundary, which rules out essentially all production IIoT, smart-meter, and connected-vehicle deployments. 2) Per-entity TTL / sliding-window eviction with a documented memory budget and an explicit (device_id × channel × window) memory accounting — device-id × channel cardinality is the dominant operational risk and the buyer needs a 'set max RAM, evict-by-TTL-then-LRU' guarantee. 3) Native t-digest / HDR-histogram / EWMA / streaming z-score primitives documented as first-class — rolling z-score against a per-device baseline and against the fleet distribution are the two flagship anomaly features and they should not require user-level glue. 4) An MQTT / Sparkplug-B / OPC-UA ingestion adapter (or a published shim recipe) — buyers will not write this themselves and the absence is friction; an officially supported MQTT-to-beava bridge example would close most of the integration gap. 5) Triggers / 'fire when counter crosses threshold' — anomaly windows literally exist to fire actions; polling 20–80 features per device every second is wasteful at fleet scale, and an in-server trigger surface would be a major differentiator vs. the Kafka+Flink stack. 6) Multi-tenancy: per-tenant namespaces, quotas, per-tenant rate-limit accounting so IoT platform vendors can embed beava across many customer fleets. 7) In-process or sidecar sharding by key prefix (device_id hash, site_id) for tenants that exceed a single box (~1M devices or ~684k EPS). 8) Replication and follower reads for the cybersecurity / safety-critical slice where a single-node restart blip is unacceptable. 9) An optional event-archive sink (S3 / Parquet / Iceberg) so the warehouse / lakehouse layer can be populated without forcing the buyer to dual-write. 10) A documented identity-stitch story for (anonymous_device_id → registered_device_id on provisioning) for consumer-IoT and unprovisioned-meter scenarios. 11) Sparkplug-B birth / death / NDEATH semantics support — connectivity-session windowing should be aware of the broker's last-will message, not just inactivity timeout. 12) Schema evolution: telemetry schemas change with every firmware rev; the @bv.event story needs to tolerate adding / renaming sensor channels without dropping state.
risk_and_non_goals.trigger_action_required: Yes, dominantly. The entire point of an anomaly window is to fire an action — open a CMMS ticket, page on-call, throttle the device, raise a SCADA alarm, route the vehicle to a diagnostic bay, dispatch a meter technician. Polling 20–80 features per device every second for threshold evaluation across a 100k-device fleet is wasteful; an in-server trigger surface is the differentiating capability vs. the Kafka+Flink incumbent. A few sub-slices need only feature serving (the ML inference scorer is reading anyway because it scores on a fixed cadence), but the rules-engine / alerting slice is action-bound.
